clinicalPearls: An acquired focal dilatation of a retinal arteriole, usually within the first three orders of branching and often along the superotemporal arcade
Typically affects elderly, hypertensive patients and is more common in women
May be asymptomatic and found incidentally, or cause visual loss through exudative maculopathy or haemorrhage

The hallmark of a ruptured macroaneurysm is haemorrhage at multiple retinal levels simultaneously, which may be sub-retinal, intraretinal, sub-internal limiting membrane (pre-retinal) and into the vitreous
The exudative form produces macular oedema and a ring of hard exudate that can threaten the fovea
Fluorescein angiography shows a fusiform or round dilatation of the arteriole with variable leakage
Many lesions thrombose and involute spontaneously, so management ranges from observation to focal laser or intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy when the macula is threatened
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic hypertension and arteriosclerosis weaken the wall of a retinal arteriole, producing a focal saccular or fusiform dilatation. The abnormal vessel may leak plasma, causing macular oedema and hard exudate, or it may rupture, releasing blood that can dissect into several retinal planes at once, giving the characteristic multilevel haemorrhage. Some macroaneurysms undergo spontaneous thrombosis and sclerosis, involuting without treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Coats disease and other retinal telangiectasia
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to locate the arteriolar dilatation and characterise the haemorrhage
Optical coherence tomography to assess macular oedema and the level of haemorrhage
Fluorescein angiography to confirm the fusiform arteriolar dilatation and demonstrate leakage
Optical coherence tomography angiography or indocyanine green angiography when the view is obscured by blood
Blood pressure measurement and cardiovascular risk assessment
B-scan ultrasound if dense vitreous haemorrhage prevents fundus examination
redFlags: Dense vitreous haemorrhage obscuring the fundus
Multiple or bilateral lesions suggesting significant systemic vascular disease
reference.prognosis: The outlook is often favourable, as many macroaneurysms involute spontaneously; the visual outcome depends chiefly on whether the fovea is involved by exudate or haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesion for wet age-related macular degeneration and committing to unnecessary long-term injections
Failing to identify and treat underlying hypertension
Misattributing an unexplained vitreous haemorrhage in an elderly patient
Over-treating a lesion that is already thrombosing and involuting
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
management: Observe asymptomatic or non-foveal lesions, as many macroaneurysms thrombose and involute spontaneously
Control the underlying hypertension and cardiovascular risk factors that drive arteriolar wall damage
Treat sight-threatening exudative maculopathy with focal laser photocoagulation and/or intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
Manage dense vitreous haemorrhage by observation or pars plana vitrectomy, and consider Nd:YAG membranotomy or pneumatic displacement for premacular haemorrhage
Monitor with optical coherence tomography and fundus examination for macular oedema and resolution
Refer to a medical retina specialist for treatment decisions and to address systemic vascular risk
